Endometrial polyps can be found in both pre-menopausal and post-menopausal women, although they tend to affect older women. Research suggests that pre- and post-menopausal endometrial polyps exhibit different hormone receptor and proliferation markers.

Pre-menopausal polyps are thought to have lost the usual control mechanisms for apoptotic regulation due to their hormonal milieu. This may contribute to their growth.

Post-menopausal polyps, on the other hand, appear to still have some level of control over apoptosis, but this is not as effective as it once was.

While there are differences between pre- and post-menopausal endometrial polyps, both groups share similar hormone receptor and proliferation markers. This suggests that there may be a common underlying mechanism driving the development of these polyps, regardless of their age at diagnosis.

However, it's essential to note that while some genetic variations may influence the risk or behavior of endometrial polyps, more research is needed to fully understand the complex relationships between hormonal factors, genetic predisposition, and polyp growth.
